alignment.note: The Vulgate transmits an introductory clause auditum est quod in domo esset ('it was heard that he was at home'), reflecting a Greek variant tradition reading ἠκούσθη ὅτι ἐν οἴκῳ ἐστίν. Neither the NA28 text printed here nor the Peshitta attest this clause, which softens the abruptness of the gathering.

The Greek εὐθέως ('immediately') has no counterpart in either the Peshitta or the Vulgate, both of which proceed directly to the gathering. This adverb is a hallmark of Markan style but is here unrepresented in the versions.
συνήχθησαν / ܐܬܟܢܫܘ (root k-n-sh) / convenerunt all render the aorist/perfect passive 'were gathered together' with equivalent force.
ὥστε / ܐܝܟܢܐ / ita ut introduce the consecutive 'so that' clause; the Latin uses the standard two-word correlative construction.

Greek expresses the result impersonally with the infinitive χωρεῖν ('there was no longer room'), as does the Latin caperet; the Peshitta recasts the clause personally and transitively, ܕܠܐ ܐܫܟܚ ܐܚܕ ܐܢܘܢ ('so that [the place] could not hold them'), supplying an explicit object pronoun ܐܢܘܢ. The constructions are semantically equivalent but syntactically divergent.

Greek substantivizes the prepositional phrase with the neuter article (τὰ πρὸς τὴν θύραν, 'the [spaces] about the door'); both Peshitta (ܩܕܡ ܬܪܥܐ) and Vulgate (ad januam) render only the bare prepositional phrase, omitting the articular substantivization characteristic of the Greek.
καί / ܘ- (prefixed to ܡܡܠܠ) / et, coordinating conjunction.

Greek ἐλάλει is a synthetic imperfect; Latin loquebatur matches it morphologically; the Peshitta forms the durative past periphrastically with participle plus the auxiliary ܡܡܠܠ ܗܘܐ, a standard Syriac means of expressing continuous past action.
αὐτοῖς / ܥܡܗܘܢ / eis; the Syriac uses the comitative 'with them' where Greek and Latin use the dative 'to them'.
